A few months ago,@sh_reya and I released eval skills plugin. We iterated on it a bunch and recently made it better  

The biggest change is a new error-discovery skill. Give your coding agent a file of AI outputs or traces, and it builds a custom review app w/intelligent sampling. As you annotate the sample, the agent groups your notes into failure modes and finds related examples.  

We also added a start skill, which looks at your situation and routes your agent to the right workflow. It can help you find errors in a set of traces or audit an eval pipeline you already have.

rt_of.author: viticci
rt_of.text:
It's honestly remarkable how good *and* unique Codex Remote for iOS is.

Other companies' "remote control" features force you to start from a Mac (Claude, Cursor). 

Codex Remote is, as far as I know, the only one with full start-from-iOS flow, near desktop parity, and a voice mode.

I coordinate dozens of threads from iOS on a daily basis. The voice mode is especially impressive since it can dispatch to individual threads, load all your context + plugin/skills from desktop, and even reopen threads on-screen.

I recently set up a second Mac mini (a Tahoe machine for backwards compatibility of my CLIs) and Codex Remote voice mode guided me through the process of setting up a Comet Remote KVM while I was wearing AirPods. While speaking to Codex on my iPhone, it operated a connected Fingerbot and told me what cables to attach and how. Honestly felt like the future. (Pictured: a Linux Mini PC Codex also set up for me.)

(My second favorite as an iOS user: T3 Code on iOS by @theo and team. Super smooth onboarding flow with T3 Connect and I love the multi-harness nature of it. Wish it had a voice mode!)

Some wishes for Codex Remote:

- Home Screen widgets to launch Codex Remote and its voice mode 
- Proper integrations with iOS frameworks (Reminders, Calendar, etc.)
- Integration with Files app (mount local iOS folders)

Overall, probably my favorite iOS feature in a long time. Nothing else quite like it right now.

rt_of.author: Pragmatic_Eng
rt_of.text:
What is intentional compaction? @DexHorthy, founder of HumanLayer, explains:

“When context is noisy, you deliberately compress the useful parts into a clear markdown artifact, verify it, and then start a fresh conversation.

Frequent intentional compaction is the building block for building software with AI. How do we get the most out of today’s models, how do we control what we’re putting into the context window so we get the best results, which means doing as much work as possible in the smart zone, the first hundred thousand tokens.

1. The research step: we go read a bunch of code and turn it into a doc: that’s our compaction. We take that forward.

2. In the next session we read the ticket and the intent and turn that into a design document: here’s the high-level current state, desired end state, and a bunch of design questions.

3. Then you take the research and the design and you do a new session, new context: you’ve compressed the intent, and you’ve compressed the state of the codebase, so you can then do your planning.”

items.author: mitchellh
items.text:
Good moment today to remind everyone to stay frosty with AI. I was working on making a server stoppable via the CLI, and Codex decided the best path forward was to implement an unauthenticated network API to every server to shut itself down. Excellent work.

I responded with "I don't know about that." (I usually give more direct feedback but this was so absurd) and it thought for like 20 seconds and responded "Server stopping should not be part of an unauthenticated network API." Yes. lol. 

By the way, the result I was looking for was that we automatically start a locally discovery Unix-socket bound server so I wanted it to discover that (using prior mechanisms already made) and gracefully stop that. 

The driver is absolutely accountable here (me). My lazy prompting led AI to think I wanted to be able to stop ANY configured server I was talking to. Shame on me for thinking it was obvious here. But, I also reviewed it and found this idiocy, so, that's where good AI drivers come in. Also me.

items.author: mitchellh
items.text:
I've moved on to optimizing libghostty Wasm runtime memory usage and I am learning a lot! The first discovery: Zig's `std.heap.MemoryPool` is very bad for Wasm! We replaced it with a custom Wasm-specific pool that lowered libghostty's required terminal memory by 75% without any measurable throughput impact.

Some background: `std.heap.MemoryPool` is a very high performance memory pool implementation for identically sized items directly in the Zig standard library. For non-wasm targets, its very good! We use it a lot!

But there is a major problem due to the interaction of two separate behaviors: first, the Zig std memory pool grows by 1.5x whenever it has no free space. To grow, it asks the backing allocator, which is usually general-purpose. On Wasm targets, that general-purpose allocator is the BrkAllocator which grows by power-of-two for big allocation slots (what we were hitting).

On native (non-wasm) targets, this just gets increasingly large virtual memory allocations, which is fine! Good, even! Virtual memory mappings are cheap and the total mapped memory isn't resident/physical until it's used. Allocation syscalls are expensive and its better to get too much.

But wasm is not like that. Every linear memory growth is immediately measured, zeroed, resident memory. Second, memory growth doesn't require a "syscall" in the same sense/overhead of the word. 

The result is you get really big linear memory growth in WebAssembly and it looks/feels bad in web inspector and saves absolutely nothing on future IO.

We replaced it with a very simple pool (~20 lines of effective code) that grows the linear memory by exactly 1 item size when it needs it and maintains a module-global free list (assumes single-threaded Wasm module) so same-item pools are shared globally.

PR here: https://t.co/1Uh2yPk9fn

Retrieve more, rerank, get better results. That's what most of us expect from search, but it turns out to be wrong! 🤯

I'm SUPER EXCITED to publish the 141st episode of the Weaviate Podcast with Mathew Jacob (@mat_jacob1002)! Mathew led the work behind "Drowning in Documents" during his time at Databricks and is now a Ph.D. student at the University of Washington working on ML systems!

This episode dives deep into "Drowning in Documents". This has been one of the most influential papers for us @weaviate_io as we are exploring scaling reranked retrieval. I think it is a must read for those working in Search and Information Retrieval. 🙌

We begin with an overview of the paper, and then dive into full scoring with cross encoders and phantom hits. We then cover Listwise Rerankers, what next generation cross encoders might look like, and ranking cascades.

On the topic of ranking cascades, I loved learning about Mathew’s work with Melissa Pan (@melissapan), Negar Arabzadeh (@NegarEmpr) and collaborators on “Natural Language Query to Configuration for Retrieval Agents”. Per-query “effort” prediction is certainly going to be a huge component on the future of these search systems! (Congratulations to OpenRouter 😆)

We then dove into Mathew’s work on TraceLab, a super exciting effort to understand coding agents such as Claude Code and Codex. ⌨️

This was a super fun conversation, and I really hope you find it useful!
YouTube: https://t.co/3lPicYhk5R
Spotify: https://t.co/sx0o06kilI

A thing missing from policy talk over AI is clear description about (1) what uses of AI are good, (2) which uses could be good with the right policy regime, (3) which non-catastrophic bad uses require regulation to mitigate & (4) which catastrophic uses require preemptive action

2. Scientists watched a single-celled organism evolve multicellularity in real time.

After researchers introduced a predator, a single-cell alga evolved into a multicellular organism. The transition reportedly took about a year—a compressed demonstration of how environmental pressure can produce a major evolutionary transition.

https://t.co/SpZIVNPUbA

3. The human brain contains billions of neurons but appears to process conscious thought at roughly ten bits per second.

This paper asks why our enormous biological machinery produces such a narrow stream of conscious processing—and why we can generally think about only one thing at a time.

https://t.co/E1g7ffUhK7

4. Leaded gasoline may have reduced the cognitive ability of about half the American population.

A study estimated the population-scale impact of childhood lead exposure from automobile exhaust. It is a remarkable example of a mundane technology quietly imposing enormous social costs.

https://t.co/51asPa5sF3

5. Cats may exploit change blindness to sneak up on us.

Change blindness is our failure to notice even dramatic environmental changes while our attention is elsewhere. This post connects the phenomenon to a familiar feline behavior: moving closer whenever you look away.

https://t.co/3WWWa6MkjX

6. When did modern civilization finally surpass the technological achievements of the ancient world?

The answer was far less obvious to people living in 1599 or even 1715 than it seems today. This essay reconstructs how early-modern thinkers assessed their own technology relative to antiquity.

https://t.co/SCwuAZTKnz

7. People in nearly every generation believe that morality is declining.

Even young people often believe that today’s generation is worse than those that came before it. Research on the “illusion of moral decline” suggests that this recurring perception is produced by predictable biases in memory and attention.

https://t.co/FeV5NFLZoM

8. Here is a recreation of an entire GPT architecture inside a spreadsheet.

It is a working nanoGPT with approximately 85,000 parameters, small enough to fit inside a spreadsheet file. Because the data and parameters are visible, it turns an otherwise opaque transformer model into something you can inspect cell by cell.

https://t.co/kKfyNzjvXr

9. Studying the brain’s hardware may not explain human intelligence any more than studying computer hardware explains Excel pivot tables.

This paper argues that human intelligence cannot be understood independently of accumulated culture. Much of what makes an individual capable exists outside the individual—in tools, institutions, norms, and knowledge inherited from other people.

https://t.co/qX1STumeqH

10. When AI became better than humans at Go, human players subsequently became better too.

Professional Go players began learning from strategies discovered by machines, producing an unusual example of superhuman AI expanding rather than simply replacing human capability.

https://t.co/dDHJFDp4iK

11. The familiar integer values assigned to chess pieces are convenient—but not really correct.

A pawn is worth one, a bishop or knight roughly three, and a rook five. But a game as contextual as chess should not yield perfectly tidy integer values. This thread investigates what the pieces are actually worth.

https://t.co/C6uzo3TYTi

12. There is film of Paul McCartney going from almost nothing to the beginnings of a hit song in roughly 45 seconds.

It is a rare chance to watch creative expertise operating in real time: not merely performing or explaining a finished work, but discovering it.

https://t.co/hfcDriBzAI

13. What if The Lord of the Rings had emerged from ancient China?

An artist reimagined Frodo and the Fellowship through the visual language of ancient China. It is not merely a costume swap; it demonstrates how strongly world-building depends on an underlying cultural vocabulary.

https://t.co/p2ZqsFZ3Nn

14. Why does the post-scarcity civilization in Iain M. Banks’s Culture novels remain so compelling?

“Why the Culture Wins” examines the political and philosophical appeal of Banks’s civilization—and why it feels like more than a conventional science-fiction utopia.

https://t.co/kPDFGy2yhA

15. The University of Chicago offers a four-year Great Books discussion course that is open to anyone.

The program provides a structured route through foundational works without requiring enrollment in a degree. Andy Matuschak completed its first year and shared his observations.

https://t.co/xFJIDt6j9T

16. A collection of rules that produced exactly the opposite of their intended effects.

One example: banning alcohol inside college football stadiums led fans to drink more beforehand, increasing intoxication problems. The thread collects similar cases in which incentives and adaptation defeated seemingly sensible policies.

https://t.co/MGeULUpscC

17. Here are 29 slides explaining the plot of Tenet.

The post is funny, but it is also an impressive exercise in visual explanation: taking a deliberately disorienting film about inverted time and attempting to make its causal structure comprehensible.

https://t.co/B64i0MynwD

18. This graphic compares how quickly every planet rotates—and the direction each one points.

Jupiter spins at a remarkable speed, while Venus barely turns at all and rotates in the opposite direction from most planets. It makes the solar system feel less like a tidy diagram and more like a collection of wildly different physical worlds.

https://t.co/gJJrZ6QFd0

19. Mario games demonstrate that two mechanically similar experiences can feel psychologically different.

The example is a compact lesson in design: objective similarity does not produce subjective equivalence. Presentation, framing, feedback, and context can transform how the same underlying structure feels.

https://t.co/poMnBhaZCV

20. An AI learned to defeat elite human poker players in a game of hidden information.

Unlike chess or Go, poker requires reasoning about uncertainty, deception, and opponents who know things you do not. Pluribus decisively beat five professionals across 10,000 hands, making it an unusually important—and still underappreciated—AI result.

https://t.co/w5PL6jlLvL

21. An open-source tool can turn any city into a minimalist map poster.

Choose a place and generate a clean, highly detailed visual from its street network. It is a lovely example of public geographic data becoming personal art.

https://t.co/Vb9GujDju3

22. A mostly complete visual map of neural-network architectures.

The field contains far more varieties than the phrase “neural network” suggests. This graphic organizes many of them into a single taxonomy, making decades of architectural experimentation visible at once.

https://t.co/pHmpnC0k8Y

rt_of.author: aiDotEngineer
rt_of.text:
🆕 Context Engineering in 2026: Compaction, Memory & Cost

https://t.co/08qPA63bBd

@Whats_AI, @samridhivaid and @omar_solano1 return!

This workshop is about engineering the context window so rot stops happening, shown with @towards_AI's open-source AI tutor, which answers questions for students of our AI-engineering courses. 

Context engineering is deciding what the model sees on every single call — instructions, history, retrieved course content, memory, and tool outputs — and it's the line between a tutor that holds a coherent session and one that forgets the student's setup halfway through. 

We'll move in three stages, mirroring how the project actually went. The concepts: 

- the two root problems (a finite window, a stateless model), 
- the full compaction toolkit (truncation, trimming, tool-result clearing, summarization, and offloading to files — and when each actually helps), 
- memory that survives across sessions, skills loaded on demand, and 
- production-grade retrieval (chunking, metadata, course scoping, hybrid search, reranking, and evaluating). 

We'll cover the tutor's architecture, and the evaluation harness we used to measure every run on Gemini — tokens, cost, latency, and memory probes instead of vibe-checks. At real volume, even Gemini Flash got expensive, so we tested whether open and local models could match the quality for a fraction of the cost and match result quality. 

Everything is open-source and will be shared during the workshop.

items.text:
Recommended paper for agent skill builders.

There are 56,804 public agent skills today, all competing for fewer than 100 reliable trigger slots in the system prompt. Your own playbooks compete for that same space, and the long tail never gets used.

skills separates the three things installation bundles together. Content, persistence, and automatic triggering. Only triggering needs to sit in the prompt.

A path addresses any skill, subtree, or collection, and reading it is enough to use it. A directory becomes a menu, so bundles stop being all-or-nothing. Vendoring copies a skill into your Git tree at the same path, so your team owns and adapts it.

No manifest, no lockfile, no registration, and SKILL.md is unchanged.

items.author: omarsar0
items.text:
Interesting paper demystifying agent skills.

If you maintain skills for your agent, this one is worth your time.

(bookmark it)

Skills are usually assumed to inject knowledge the model lacks. However, this paper finds something interesting.

Across 8,135 normalized trial records, procedural anchoring accounts for 65.7% of cases where a skill helps, and explicit knowledge injection accounts for 4.5%. Skills stabilize execution rather than supply facts.

As the pool grows from 5 to 100 skills, actual-use precision falls from 29.6% to 3.3%.

Skills still beat Workflow Memory by 6.06 points in matched comparisons, and they break under brittle assumptions, incompatible contexts, or insufficient adaptation.

Paper: https://t.co/BRo32B4GXY

rt_of.author: omarsar0
rt_of.text:
Interesting new research from IBM.

If you pick models from benchmark deltas, some of that delta belongs to the phrasing rather than the model.

BenchDrift generates meaning-preserving variations of benchmark problems along linguistic, referential, pragmatic, and structural axes, holding the answer fixed, then measures how often correctness flips.

Phrasing sensitivity does not fade as models improve. It changes sign. Weak models gain more from rephrasing than they lose, while strong models lose far more than they gain, so the top models on a benchmark are the ones whose scores depend most on the wording they happened to receive.

Fragility also belongs to the rephrasing. Across eight models on GSM8K, MMLU, and MATH-Hard, they largely agree on which rephrasings cost the most correct answers even while differing in how much they drift overall.

Rephrasing breaks answers models were confident about, whether the problem gets shorter or longer.

Paper: https://t.co/69JlAwXcev

items.author: rasbt
items.text:
Clarification here. Somewhere in the comments, I agreed that one might have to rerun the LLM for checking for watermarks. That's not correct.

I am not 100% which exact technique they use, but they mentioned that they base their method on the SynthID-Text method from https://t.co/1YdFP3vnNQ

So, in that method, they have so-called watermarking functions that give 1’s for certain terms and 0’s for others, and then they do a tournament-style selection. 

Those that survive have a lot of 1’s, i.e., are high-scoring.
So, to later check if a text is watermarked, they basically just have to (re)apply the watermarking functions to some text and if it’s above a score threshold (which you reach if you have a lot of those watermark-words that score highly), then the text is likely watermarked.

I.e., you don’t need to rerun the LLM to check, just the “cheap” watermark functions (it’s kind of like hashing).

items.author: cwolferesearch
items.text:
I’m a big fan of smaller MoE models, and NVIDIA’s Nemotron 3.5 lightning is a great release in this space…

NVIDIA is expanding the suite / offering of Nemotron models to be quite comprehensive. Now, Nemotron includes a smaller MoE model (30B parameters, 3B active), which provides better support for use cases that require high throughput / low latency.

AI research is moving away from using frontier models for everything. For long-running agentic tasks, it doesn’t make sense to use a frontier-level reasoning model for every step of the task. Instead, we should use a powerful model for planning / orchestration and delegate sub-tasks to faster / efficient agents that can better handle execution.

Nemotron 3.5 lightning focuses on this area, providing a model optimized for the high-volume execution layer of agentic tasks; e.g., validating tool outputs, executing commands, solving simpler sub-tasks, etc. The model is also specifically trained for agentic use cases and compatibility with popular agent frameworks / harnesses (e.g., hermes / openclaw).

“Frontier reasoning models such as Nemotron 3 Ultra handle orchestration and complex planning while smaller, more efficient models handle the high-volume execution layer.” - Nemotron 3.5 Lightning blog

To support even better inference efficiency, Nemotron 3.5 lightning is also trained with multi-token prediction to enable speculative decoding. The release also includes drafters for DSpark / DFlash (and quantized checkpoints) to enable further inference optimizations.

Nemotron 3.5 Lightning achieves impressive results on the accuracy-speed frontier. It has 4x inference speed of similar-size models. On the artificial analysis intelligence index, we can see that Nemotron 3.5 Lightning achieves impressive performance for the speed category it is in (kind of a region of its own).

Inference-optimized small MoE models are so useful for practical tasks. There are tons of use cases that can be solved by post-training a small, fast model to reach very high levels of reliability at low costs. Plus, NVIDIA provides several finetuning recipes that can be used with 3.5 lightning out of the box.
